source: Project: Video Platform Data Analysis
text:
Video Platform Data Analysis (2025) for AI gaming clip platform. Behavior and growth deep dive for an AI gaming clip platform: activation levers that move retention and clip output.
Categories: Data Analyst, Dashboard. Stack: SQL, Python, Tableau, Pitch Deck.
Context
An AI assistant for gaming creators that auto-turns long gameplay streams into highlight clips. It sits between gameplay capture and social distribution (TikTok, YouTube Shorts, Reels), so every onboarded creator either becomes a recurring clip source or churns silently. Growth had plateaued, and the founding team wanted to know whether the bottleneck was acquisition, activation, or content output per creator.
 Problem
Internal dashboards reported headline numbers but missed the cohort view. Three questions the team couldn't answer with confidence:
- Which onboarding step quietly bleeds the most users before they generate a clip?
- Do power creators behave differently from the median in week one of the AI clip generator?
- Where does the funnel break for users who connect gameplay capture but never publish a clip?
Without that, every roadmap discussion turned into opinion.

I scoped the analysis around the pub

source: Project: Affiliate Commission Performance Review & Recovery Plan
text:
Affiliate Commission Performance Review & Recovery Plan (2026) for E-commerce affiliate platform. Root-cause analysis of a 34% commission revenue decline: funnel diagnosis, cohort retention, and a two-track recovery playbook for leadership.
Categories: Data Analyst, Pitch Deck. Stack: Python, Excel, PowerPoint, Funnel Analysis, Cohort Analysis.
Context
An e-commerce affiliate operation earning commission through video content that drives marketplace transactions. Commission revenue had fallen four months straight — a ~34% cumulative drop. Leadership needed a clear diagnosis and recovery plan before the trend turned structural.
 Problem
Three questions before scoping any fix:
- Where in the funnel (plays → impression → click → order) is volume actually leaking?
- Is the decline a rate problem (CVR/CTR falling) or a volume problem (fewer plays/impressions)?
- Are there internal levers (commission mix, SKU sourcing, retention) to recover revenue without external brand subsidies?
 Data & preparation
The funnel (plays → impression → click → order), commission, and cohort data came from the platform's internal database exports. Before any analysis, I cleaned and reconciled the raw extrac

source: Project: Affiliate Commission Performance Review & Recovery Plan
text:
l (plays → impression → click → order), commission, and cohort data came from the platform's internal database exports. Before any analysis, I cleaned and reconciled the raw extracts:
- Deduplicated transaction records and handled null/missing values across the funnel tables.
- Reconciled funnel-stage counts whose sources didn't align (plays/impressions vs click/order systems), so each stage compared on a consistent base.
- Normalized dates into consistent monthly cohorts (January–April).
- Standardized commission rates and Rupiah amounts (direct vs indirect, standard ~2% vs extra ~4% tiers) into a single clean schema.
 Approach
1. Built a full-funnel comparison (January baseline vs April) across plays, impressions, clicks, and orders, isolating the bottleneck at each stage.
2. Decomposed commission into direct vs indirect channels — indirect (clicking one SKU but buying another) carried 97% of revenue and 99% of the decline.
3. Analyzed CTR and CVR independently: CTR was flat, confirming the problem was purchase intent (CVR had dropped meaningfully), not attention.
4. Ran cohort retention across Jan–Mar cohorts, surfacing a significant collapse in month-1 retention — the most alar

source: Project: Affiliate Commission Performance Review & Recovery Plan
text:
purchase intent (CVR had dropped meaningfully), not attention.
4. Ran cohort retention across Jan–Mar cohorts, surfacing a significant collapse in month-1 retention — the most alarming structural signal.
5. Found the commission-mix lever: a minority of orders earned the higher-tier rate, so shifting the mix toward better-tier SKUs could recover meaningful monthly revenue at existing volume.
6. Packaged findings into a 10-slide executive deck with a two-track recovery plan (quick wins 0–60 days, structural levers 60–180 days) and three leadership asks.
 Outcome
The deck became the working document for Q2 planning. Three decisions followed:
- Immediate: Product approved a 3-day SKU refresh cycle (down from 7) to combat ad fatigue, and began testing personalized SKU recommendations to recover CVR.
- Short-term: BD prioritized targeted-affiliate negotiations with priority brands to unlock higher commission tiers.
- Structural: Growth scoped a retention program for the Jan–Mar cohorts before the active base shrank further.
Projected recovery, if all three tracks execute: 50–70% of the monthly gap within two quarters.

- No conversion funnel: Offline workshops existed in the market but lacked digital funnels to convert casual viewers into paying participants.
- Monetization without erosion: Any revenue mod

source: Project: Nuclear Energy Policy Discourse Network Analysis
text:
Nuclear Energy Policy Discourse Network Analysis (2025) for Policy Research Initiative. Scraping news + social media on Indonesia's nuclear policy, then Gemini-powered DNA + SNA + sentiment analysis dashboard.
Categories: AI Engineer, Data Science, Data Engineer. Stack: Gemini API, GCP, Sentiment Analysis, MongoDB, pyvis.
Context
A policy research initiative on Indonesia's nuclear and EBET (new and renewable energy) debate. The team had a research design but no production-grade pipeline to collect, parse, and visualize the discourse at scale. The deliverable: a proof of concept combining Discourse Network Analysis (DNA), Social Network Analysis (SNA), and sentiment scoring across news and social platforms.
 Problem
Classical content analysis wouldn't scale to the volume needed. Four blockers:
- Heterogeneous sources — news and social posts scraped from multiple sites, each with its own structure, pagination, and rate limits.
- Articles spanned Indonesian and English with code-mixing, breaking off-the-shelf NLP.
- Manual coding of actor, claim, stance, and sentiment was the bottleneck, not collection.
- The team needed a defensible overview of where the conversation stands, not a du

source: Project: Nuclear Energy Policy Discourse Network Analysis
text:

- Manual coding of actor, claim, stance, and sentiment was the bottleneck, not collection.
- The team needed a defensible overview of where the conversation stands, not a dump of charts.
 Approach
1. Built scraping pipelines for news results (keywords: nuclear, EBET, RUU EBET variants) and relevant social posts, normalized into one MongoDB schema with source provenance.
2. Used the Gemini API to extract actor, claim, stance, frame, and sentiment per item, with a prompt template tuned against a manually coded gold set to keep LLM output comparable to analyst coding.
3. Built two network views — actor-to-claim (DNA) and actor-to-actor co-occurrence (SNA) — persisted as edge lists and merged with sentiment so each edge carries polarity.
4. Rendered interactive networks (pyvis, Chart.js) plus sentiment timelines as a static HTML report bundle.
5. Ran the pipeline on ~1,000 items across two snapshot windows to compare discourse shifts over time.
 Outcome

source: Project: Regional Writing Ecosystem Index (PCA)
text:
Regional Writing Ecosystem Index (PCA) (2024) for Cultural Policy Think Tank. PCA-based composite model (68.2% variance) analyzing regional writing ecosystem strength across Indonesia.
Categories: Data Science, Data Analyst. Stack: scikit-learn, PCA, Looker Studio, Statistical Analysis.
Context
A cultural policy think tank needed a defensible way to compare regional writing ecosystems across Indonesia. The think tank supplied its own internal dataset of regional indicators — certified writers, publishing activity, and literacy proxies — but had no single index that could rank provinces in a way policymakers would accept.
 Problem
Single indicators told contradictory stories. Three issues:
- Indicators were on different scales and units, so straight summation was meaningless.
- Some variables were highly correlated, double-counting if left untreated.
- The output had to be one composite score that survived academic review.
 Approach
1. Curated and cleaned the variable set across provinces, including LSP (certified writer/editor) counts at the regency level.
2. Normalized variables with z-scores, then ran a correlation audit to flag redundancy.
3. Applied PCA, selected the first two

source: Project: Regional Writing Ecosystem Index (PCA)
text:
ertified writer/editor) counts at the regency level.
2. Normalized variables with z-scores, then ran a correlation audit to flag redundancy.
3. Applied PCA, selected the first two components from the scree plot and cumulative variance, and validated the loadings against domain expectation.
4. Reconstructed a composite Writing Ecosystem Index from the component scores and ranked provinces.
5. Packaged the methodology, index, and province ranking into a report and slide narrative for the think tank's policy audience.
 Outcome
The first two principal components captured 68.2% of variance, with loadings mapping cleanly to a production axis and a professionalization axis. The index ranked provinces defensibly, and the composite score plus methodology became the analytical core of the public-facing report.

Categories: Data Engineer. Stack: Python, Cloud Run, GCS, APIFY, Flask, Docker.
Context
A marketing research team needed continuous profile and content data from five social platforms to feed campaign benchmarking and influencer scoping. The existing setup was a patchwork of one-off notebooks per platform — each rerun needed manual stitching, and any mid-batch failure meant starting from scratch.
 Problem
- Five platforms, five auth models, rate limits, and content schemas — a separate script each meant five failure modes for ops.
- Batches over a few thousand accounts routinely failed mid-run; without checkpointing, the whole run restarted, burning quota and time.
- Output scattered across local CSVs with no consistent naming made downstream analysis brittle.
 Approach
1. Designed a three-layer modular architecture — parsers (URL normalization), collectors (platform API calls), models (canonical profile + content shape) — so adding a sixth platform is three small classes, not a pipeline refactor.

text:
Google News Scraping + Gemini AI Aggregation (2025) for Macro research desk. Always-on macro news scraping pipeline on Cloud Run combining Google CSE, APIFY, and Gemini parsing.
Categories: AI Engineer, Data Engineer. Stack: Python, Google CSE, APIFY, Gemini API, Cloud Run, Web Scraping.
Context
A small research desk tracking monetary policy and FX needed continuous coverage of Bank Indonesia, inflation, and rupiah-related news across Indonesian and English sources. Manual scanning was the bottleneck — by the time an analyst had read enough to brief the team, intraday signals were already stale.
 Problem
Three constraints shaped the build:
- Coverage had to be intraday — a daily digest wasn't enough.
- The Google CSE API caps results at 100 per query and deep paging at index 91, so a naive scheduler would miss articles or burn quota.
- Search results return only titles, snippets, and links — article bodies had to be fetched separately, then parsed into structured fields analysts could query.
 Approach
1. Built a single-purpose Cloud Run scraper that hits the CSE API on a configurable window (5–60 min), filters by after: date plus a strict in-code timestamp check, and writes dedupli

source: Project: Google News Scraping + Gemini AI Aggregation
text:
Built a single-purpose Cloud Run scraper that hits the CSE API on a configurable window (5–60 min), filters by after: date plus a strict in-code timestamp check, and writes deduplicated records to monthly JSON files ( articles YYYY-MM.json ) via a checkpoint store.
2. Triggered it from Cloud Scheduler so cadence is decoupled from code; queries and intervals are env vars, so the team tunes coverage per topic without redeploying.

source: Project: Debt Collection Analytics & Agent Productivity

Categories: Data Analyst, Dashboard. Stack: Python, Pandas, Excel, Looker Studio.
Context
A banking collections operation: hundreds of agents, a large-scale delinquent portfolio.  Problem
- Ten monthly Excel workbooks (Feb–Nov 2025), each with its own quirks: header drift, merged cells, inconsistent agent name spellings.
- Alarming headline numbers — an extremely high unconnected rate and a success rate well below industry benchmarks — needed a defensible explanation, not just the metric.
- One agent had anomalous numbers (zero connected calls but the highest "paid count") that would distort any naive ranking and undermine trust in the dashboard.

- "Need per cylinder" vs "stock OVH" was a per-row Excel calc with no aggregated view to flag shortages before they hit scheduling.
- Planning wanted one screen showing which unit needs what part next, but the source data was structured for parts catalogs, not forward planning.

source: Project: Mobile App Analytics Data Pipeline
text:
Mobile App Analytics Data Pipeline (2026) for Digital financial services app. Multi-source ingestion pipeline unifying AppsFlyer, MoEngage, Google Play Console, and App Store Connect into BigQuery for a Looker Studio monitoring dashboard.
Categories: Data Engineer. Stack: Python, dbt, BigQuery, Cloud Run Jobs, Cloud Workflows, Cloud Scheduler, Cloud Build, GCP Secret Manager, Terraform, Looker Studio.
Context
A digital financial services app needed a single source of truth for their product analytics. Data was scattered across four platforms: AppsFlyer (attribution and events), MoEngage (push campaigns), Google Play Console (Android performance), and App Store Connect (iOS analytics). Each had its own API format, auth method, and data lag. Marketing, product, and growth teams were pulling reports manually from each platform individually.
The goal was to automate all four sources into one BigQuery warehouse, transform the raw data with dbt into clean mart tables, and surface it in a Looker Studio dashboard refreshed twice daily.
 Problem
Four distinct ingestion challenges in one pipeline:
- AppsFlyer exposes separate endpoints per report type (installs, events, cohorts, cost) across

source: Project: Mobile App Analytics Data Pipeline
text:
refreshed twice daily.
 Problem
Four distinct ingestion challenges in one pipeline:
- AppsFlyer exposes separate endpoints per report type (installs, events, cohorts, cost) across iOS and Android. That is 8 total pulls per run.
- MoEngage requires a two-step campaign API: search for campaigns first, then fetch stats per campaign.
- Google Play Console has a 3-day data lag on vitals APIs. Requesting data newer than T-3 returns HTTP 400, so the pipeline window must be offset accordingly.
- App Store Connect uses JWT-signed tokens with short expiry, requiring rotation logic baked into the extractor.
Beyond ingestion, the pipeline needed CI/CD, environment isolation (dev vs. prod), and a runbook a non-engineer could follow for token rotation and backfills.
 Approach
 Architecture. Cloud Scheduler triggers Cloud Workflows twice daily. The workflow fans out all four extractors in parallel, waits for all to succeed, then runs the dbt transform step. Each extractor runs as an independent Cloud Run Job. A single Docker image packages both the Python ingestion code and the dbt project, and each job sets its own command and args at runtime, keeping the image count to one.
 Ingestion layer. E

source: Project: Mobile App Analytics Data Pipeline
text:
Docker image packages both the Python ingestion code and the dbt project, and each job sets its own command and args at runtime, keeping the image count to one.
 Ingestion layer. Each source is a Python module with its own API client, retry logic, and schema normalization. Raw payloads land in BigQuery raw layer tables. Extraction is stateless: the pipeline accepts a date range parameter, defaulting to T-4 to T-3 to accommodate the Play Console lag.
 Transform layer. dbt handles staging (type casting, deduplication, null handling) and mart (joined, aggregated, Looker-ready) layers. Models are tested with dbt's built-in schema tests, 51 tests total across all four sources, all green before production deploy.
 CI/CD. Cloud Build runs on push to develop (deploys to dev GCP) and main (deploys to client prod GCP via VPN). Secrets are managed in GCP Secret Manager, never in code or environment variables.
 Environments. Two long-lived branches mirror two GCP projects: consultant-owned dev for testing, client-owned prod for live data. Feature branches go through dev E2E verification before merging to main.
 Results
- 4 sources fully automated across AppsFlyer, MoEngage, Google Play Console

text:

 Results
- 4 sources fully automated across AppsFlyer, MoEngage, Google Play Console, and App Store Connect, all running end-to-end in production.
- 51 dbt tests passing across all sources, covering null checks, uniqueness, accepted values, and referential integrity.
- Full handover documentation including setup guide, runbook, data catalogs per source, and contributing guide written for the client's internal team to maintain independently.
 Stack notes
- Cloud Workflows orchestrates parallel extraction with a fan-out pattern. All four sources run simultaneously and dbt only starts after all succeed. A single workflow failure stops the transform from running on partial data.
- Single Docker image for both Python ingestion and dbt reduces image management overhead. Each Cloud Run Job overrides the command at runtime.
- dbt Medallion layers (raw, staging, mart) keep transform logic modular. Adding a new source means adding one staging model and one mart model without touching existing ones.

source: Project: Personal Portfolio Website with RAG Chat
text:
Personal Portfolio Website with RAG Chat (2026) for Self-initiated. A personal portfolio built with Next.js and a Gemini-powered chat assistant that answers questions about my work using semantic retrieval over projects, experience, and skills.
Categories: AI Engineer, Data Engineer. Stack: Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Gemini API, RAG, Vercel, MDX, Framer Motion.
Context
I wanted a portfolio that could do more than just display static content. Most portfolios are one-way: the visitor has to read through everything and piece together the picture themselves. I wanted visitors to be able to ask questions and get direct answers about my work, experience, and skills without having to dig through pages manually.
The result is this site: a Next.js portfolio with a chat widget backed by a Gemini-powered RAG pipeline.
 Problem
Two challenges to solve:
- A generic LLM with no context about me would either hallucinate or give vague answers. It needed to be grounded in actual content from the portfolio.
- Dumping all portfolio content into every prompt would be slow and wasteful. The assistant needed to retrieve only the relevant pieces per question.
 Approach
 Content layer. All portfol

source: Project: Personal Portfolio Website with RAG Chat
text:
ng all portfolio content into every prompt would be slow and wasteful. The assistant needed to retrieve only the relevant pieces per question.
 Approach
 Content layer. All portfolio content lives as structured TypeScript data (experience, projects, skills) and MDX case studies. A build-time script reads all of it, splits it into chunks, embeds each chunk via Gemini's embedding model, and writes the vectors to a local JSON file.
 Retrieval. At query time, the user's question is embedded and compared against all stored vectors using cosine similarity. The top-k most relevant chunks are pulled and injected into the system prompt as grounding context.
 Generation. Gemini handles the response with a tight system prompt: answer only from the retrieved context, never hallucinate, stay scoped to questions about my work. The response streams back to the client token by token.
 Rate limiting. Two layers: per-IP (20 requests per minute) and global (200 requests per hour) to stay within the free tier and prevent abuse.
 Frontend. Next.js App Router, Tailwind CSS for styling, Framer Motion for transitions. The chat widget floats over the page and streams responses in real time. MDX powers the

source: Project: Personal Portfolio Website with RAG Chat
text:
se.
 Frontend. Next.js App Router, Tailwind CSS for styling, Framer Motion for transitions. The chat widget floats over the page and streams responses in real time. MDX powers the case study pages.
 Stack notes
- Gemini embedding model for both indexing and query-time retrieval. Keeping both on the same model avoids vector space mismatches.
- Static vector index stored as a JSON file in the repo. Simple and fast for a portfolio-scale dataset (70 chunks). No external vector DB needed.
- Streaming SSE from the API route to the client so responses appear progressively rather than waiting for the full answer.
- Vercel for deployment with serverless functions handling the chat API.

source: Project: Telco Customer Churn Prediction (Streamlit)
text:
Telco Customer Churn Prediction (Streamlit) (2022) for Self-initiated portfolio project. End-to-end ML app benchmarking Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and Gradient Boosting on telco subscriber data, deployed live on Streamlit.
Categories: Data Science, ML Engineer, Dashboard. Stack: Python, Streamlit, scikit-learn, Pandas, Logistic Regression, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting.
Context
A self-initiated project to practice the full ML lifecycle on a known business problem: predicting telecom subscriber churn. The dataset is DQLab's dummy data for a fictional "DQLab Telco" — customer state as of June 2020, ~6,800 rows, 21 attributes covering demographics, services, contract type, and billing.
The goal wasn't just to fit a model, but to make the analysis legible end-to-end: a visitor to the live app can walk through cleansing, EDA, and model comparison, then type in customer attributes and get a churn probability back.
 Problem
DQLab Telco wants to predict, ahead of time, who is likely to unsubscribe. From a modeling standpoint, three constraints:
- Imbalanced target (~26% churn, 74% non-churn), so accuracy alone misleads.
- Most predictors are categorical (gender, partner status,

source: Project: Telco Customer Churn Prediction (Streamlit)
text:
om a modeling standpoint, three constraints:
- Imbalanced target (~26% churn, 74% non-churn), so accuracy alone misleads.
- Most predictors are categorical (gender, partner status, service flags, contract terms), so encoding choices matter.
- Output must be usable — a notebook score doesn't help ops; a ten-input form returning a churn probability does.
 Approach
The Streamlit app is split into four navigable sections, each one mapping to a stage of the pipeline.
 Data cleansing. Drop operational columns (customerID, UpdatedAt), handle missing TotalCharges, standardize types. The cleaned dataset is exported to a separate CSV so EDA and modeling read from one canonical source.
 Exploratory data analysis. Bivariate plots against the Churn label — overlaid histograms for numerical features, seaborn count plots for categorical, a Plotly donut for the overall churn ratio. Three findings shaped the model framing:
- Higher monthly charges correlate with higher churn.
- Longer tenure correlates with lower churn.
- StreamingTV, InternetService, and PaperlessBilling users churn at higher rates than their counterparts, suggesting service quality or pricing friction in those segments.
 Model bu

source: Project: Telco Customer Churn Prediction (Streamlit)
text:
StreamingTV, InternetService, and PaperlessBilling users churn at higher rates than their counterparts, suggesting service quality or pricing friction in those segments.
 Model building. Label-encode non-numeric columns, split 70/30 with a fixed random state, then fit three baseline classifiers at default hyperparameters:
- Logistic Regression
- Random Forest Classifier
- Gradient Boosting Classifier
Each model surfaces its own classification report and confusion matrix in the app, with separate train/test views so the overfit pattern is visible.
 Prediction. A form takes ten attributes (gender, senior citizen, partner, tenure, phone, streaming TV, internet, paperless billing, monthly charges, total charges), encodes them as the training pipeline did, and runs them through a pickled model loaded via joblib. The app returns the predicted class plus probabilities for both outcomes.
 Results
Test accuracy was close across baselines, but training accuracy told the real story:
- Logistic Regression: 80% train / 79% test. Balanced, generalizes cleanly.
- Random Forest: 100% train / 78% test. Classic overfit signal.
- Gradient Boosting: 82% train / 79% test. Slightly better train fit, no

source: Project: Telco Customer Churn Prediction (Streamlit)
text:
/ 79% test. Balanced, generalizes cleanly.
- Random Forest: 100% train / 78% test. Classic overfit signal.
- Gradient Boosting: 82% train / 79% test. Slightly better train fit, no real test gain.
I picked Logistic Regression for production precisely because its train–test gap was smallest. Its test confusion matrix is more conservative on positives than negatives — appropriate when the downstream action (retention offers, discount budget) carries a per-customer cost you don't want to spray indiscriminately.
The operational takeaway, written into the app's Conclusion: an ML score concentrates retention spend on customers actually predicted to churn, instead of blanket promotions across the full base.
 Stack notes
- Streamlit for the entire UI — no Flask, no React. The same script runs locally and deploys to share.streamlit.io.
- scikit-learn for all three models; a uniform API across LR, RF, and GBC kept the side-by-side comparison simple.
- joblib for in-app model persistence, pickle for the saved repo artifact.
- Plotly + matplotlib + seaborn mixed deliberately: Plotly for the interactive churn donut, matplotlib for confusion matrices, seaborn for categorical count plots.
